questions.q: What is asexual reproduction in plants defined as?
a: The process resulting in the production of genetically identical offspring from one parent without the fusion of gametes
The fusion of male and female nuclei
The transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma
The germination of a seed into a seedling

questions.q: What is sexual reproduction in plants characterized by?
a: The formation of runners and tubers exclusively
The fusion of gamete nuclei (fertilization) to form a zygote, producing genetically different offspring
The division of a single cell into two identical clones
The direct growth of leaves from roots

questions.q: Which part of a flower is the female reproductive organ made of stigma, style, and ovary?
a: Stamen
Anther
Carpel (or pistil)
Filament

questions.q: What is the primary function of the anther in an insect-pollinated flower?
a: To produce sugary nectar
To receive pollen grains during pollination
To protect the flower bud before it opens
To produce and release pollen grains containing male gametes

questions.q: What are the typical structural features of insect-pollinated flowers compared to wind-pollinated flowers?
a: Brightly colored petals, scented nectar, sticky or spiky pollen grains, and enclosed stamens
Dull green petals, no scent, feathery stigmas hanging outside, and smooth lightweight pollen
Absence of any petals or sepals
Production of swimming flagellated sperm

questions.q: Which of the following describes wind-pollinated flowers?
a: They possess heavy, sticky pollen grains and large scented petals
They have dangling anthers exposed to the wind, feathery or large stigmas hanging outside the flower, and small non-colored petals without nectar
They produce sweet nectar to attract bees
They have enclosed sticky stigmas hidden deep inside petals

questions.q: What is pollination defined as?
a: The fusion of male and female gametes inside the ovule
The germination of a seed in moist soil
The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same or another flower of the same species
The dispersal of seeds away from the parent plant

questions.q: What is the difference between self-pollination and cross-pollination?
a: Self-pollination involves wind; cross-pollination involves insects
Self-pollination occurs only in artificial greenhouses
Self-pollination requires two different plants

Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or different flower on the same plant; cross-pollination involves transfer between flowers of different plants of the same species

questions.q: What happens immediately after a pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma?
a: It germinates to produce a pollen tube that grows down through the style into the ovary
It turns into a seed directly on the stigma
It absorbs sunlight to perform photosynthesis
It attracts pollinating insects

questions.q: Where does fertilization take place inside the flower's carpel?
a: Inside the anther filament
Inside an ovule within the ovary, where the male gamete nucleus fuses with the female gamete nucleus
On the surface of the sticky stigma
Inside the style canal

questions.q: What do the ovule and the ovary develop into after fertilization is complete?
a: Ovule becomes fruit; ovary becomes seed
Ovule becomes stem; ovary becomes leaf
Ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit
Ovule becomes root; ovary becomes flower

questions.q: What is seed dispersal, and why is it important for plant survival?
a: The process of seeds rotting in soil to provide fertilizer
The transport of pollen by bees to ensure fertilization
The absorption of water by dry seeds
The scattering of seeds away from the parent plant to reduce competition for light, water, and minerals

questions.q: Which of the following adaptations is typically found in seeds dispersed by the wind?
a: Lightweight structures, wing-like attachments, or parachute-like hairs (e.g., dandelion)
Sweet, fleshy, brightly colored fruit walls
Hooks or barbs that attach to animal fur
Explosive pods that twist open

questions.q: How are seeds with hooks, barbs, or sticky coats typically dispersed?
a: By water currents floating across oceans
By attaching to the fur or feathers of passing animals (epizoochory)
By wind gusts blowing them miles away
By being eaten and digested by birds

questions.q: What environmental conditions are typically required for successful seed germination?
a: Bright direct sunlight, freezing temperatures, and dry air
High concentrations of carbon dioxide and salt
Water (moisture), oxygen (for aerobic respiration), and a suitable warm temperature
Absence of any oxygen and high soil acidity

questions.q: What role does water play in the germination of a seed?
a: It acts as a food source for photosynthesis
It provides energy through anaerobic respiration
It kills dormant bacteria inside the seed
It activates enzymes, softens the testa (seed coat) to allow expansion, and allows metabolic reactions to begin

questions.q: What is the function of the cotyledon inside a seed?
a: To store food reserves (starch, protein, or oils) to nourish the young embryo seedling until it can photosynthesize
To protect the seed from insect attacks indefinitely
To absorb carbon dioxide from the air
To anchor the adult plant into deep soil

questions.q: What is the embryonic root inside a seed called?
a: Plumule
Radicle
Testa
Micropyle

questions.q: What is the embryonic shoot inside a seed called?
a: Radicle
Hypocotyl
Plumule
Cotyledon

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of artificial asexual reproduction commonly used by gardeners?
a: Seed planting in greenhouse trays
Wind pollination enhancement
Cross-breeding flower varieties
Taking stem cuttings (e.g., roses) to root in soil or water

questions.q: What is a natural method of asexual reproduction in plants involving underground swollen stems storing food?
a: Tubers (such as potatoes) or bulbs
Spore dispersal
Pollen tube growth
Zygote formation

questions.q: What advantage does asexual reproduction offer over sexual reproduction for plants in a stable environment?
a: It introduces greater genetic variation
It allows rapid production of genetically identical offspring that are already well-suited to the parent's stable habitat, without needing pollinators
It produces seeds that can survive decades of drought
It eliminates all diseases from plant populations

questions.q: What is a major disadvantage of asexual reproduction in plant populations?
a: It requires two distinct parent plants
It produces too few offspring
A sudden environmental change or disease can wipe out the entire population because all individuals are genetically identical
It depends entirely on insect pollinators

questions.q: Which part of the flower protects the unopened flower bud from mechanical damage and drying out?
a: Petals
Anther
Stigma
Sepals

questions.q: What is the role of nectar in flowers?
a: A sugary liquid secreted to attract pollinators such as insects, birds, and bats
A poison used to deter herbivores
A sticky substance used to catch wind-borne pollen
A hormone that stimulates seed germination

questions.q: Why do wind-pollinated plants produce massive quantities of pollen grains compared to insect-pollinated plants?
a: Wind pollination is 100 percent efficient
Most pollen blown by the wind is lost or fails to reach another flower of the same species, so large quantities compensate for the low probability of success
Pollen is consumed by the plant as food
Pollen acts as a fertilizer for soil

questions.q: What is the function of the micropyle in a seed?
a: To store starch reserves
To anchor the seed in the soil
A small pore in the testa that allows water to enter the seed during germination
To produce enzymes during growth

questions.q: During seed germination, why does the dry mass of the seed initially decrease before the seedling breaks through the soil surface?
a: The seed loses water through evaporation
The seed absorbs minerals from the soil
The seed sheds its testa
Food stores (like starch) are broken down and used in aerobic respiration to release energy for growth, producing carbon dioxide and water which are lost

questions.q: What happens to the dry mass of a seedling once its green leaves emerge above ground and it receives sunlight?
a: Dry mass increases as photosynthesis produces organic molecules (biomass)
Dry mass decreases continuously until the plant dies
Dry mass remains completely constant
Dry mass turns into liquid water

questions.q: Which plant organ is formed by the development of the radicle during germination?
a: Stem
Root system
Flower
Fruit

questions.q: Which plant organ is formed by the development of the plumule during germination?
a: Root cap
Seed coat
Shoot system (stem and leaves)
Anther

questions.q: What is cross-pollination generally favored in plants?
a: It requires less energy than self-pollination
It prevents flowers from opening
It ensures that only one parent plant is involved
It promotes greater genetic diversity and variation within the plant population

questions.q: What is the outer protective covering of a seed called?
a: Testa (seed coat)
Endosperm
Ovary wall
Pericarp

questions.q: Which insect is among the most common and effective pollinators for agricultural crops and flowering plants?
a: Housefly
Honeybee (*Apis mellifera*)
Mosquito
Termite

questions.q: What is vegetative propagation?
a: The growth of plants from seeds in a nursery
The artificial cross-breeding of different species
A form of asexual reproduction where new plants grow from vegetative parts like stems, roots, or leaves
The process of flowers producing pollen

questions.q: Why is oxygen necessary for seed germination?
a: To provide carbon dioxide for photosynthesis
To react with soil minerals
To act as a pesticide
To enable aerobic respiration in the embryo cells to release energy for cell division and growth
